anna-komnene.name: Anna Komnene
anna-komnene.summary: Byzantine princess and historian (1083–1153) who wrote the Alexiad, an account of her father Emperor Alexios I Komnenos's reign and a key source on the early Crusades.

simeon-seth.name: Simeon Seth
simeon-seth.summary: Byzantine scientist, translator and official, c. 1035–1110, under Emperor Michael VII Doukas, who offered early proofs that the Earth is round.

tarhana.name: Tarhana
tarhana.summary: A dried fermented food made from grain and yogurt or milk, found across Central Asian, Southeast European and Middle Eastern cuisines; known in Greek as trahanás.

mount-athos.name: Mount Athos
mount-athos.summary: Mountain and self-governing monastic region in Greece, a major center of Eastern Orthodox monastic life since at least the 9th century.

mehmed-ii.name: Mehmed II
mehmed-ii.summary: Ottoman sultan (1432–1481), known as the Conqueror, who captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, and expanded Ottoman rule across Anatolia and the Balkans.

panactum.name: Panactum
panactum.summary: An ancient fortress on the border of Attica and Boeotia, fought over by Athenians and Boeotians and captured by Demetrius I Poliorketes in 304 BC.

cretan-school.name: Cretan School
cretan-school.summary: A school of icon painting, also called post-Byzantine art, that flourished in Venetian-ruled Crete and became the central force in Greek painting from the 15th to 17th centuries; its most famous member was El Greco.

palace-of-the-grand-master-of-the-knight.name: Palace of the Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes
palace-of-the-grand-master-of-the-knight.summary: A medieval castle on the Greek island of Rhodes, one of the few examples of Gothic architecture in Greece and once the headquarters of the Knights Hospitaller.
palace-of-the-grand-master-of-the-knight.source_title: Palace of the Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes

knights-hospitaller.name: Knights Hospitaller
knights-hospitaller.summary: A Catholic military order founded in 12th-century crusader Jerusalem to care for and defend pilgrims, later based in Cyprus, Rhodes, Malta and Saint Petersburg.

byzantine-iconoclasm.name: Byzantine Iconoclasm
byzantine-iconoclasm.summary: Two periods (about 726–787 and 814–842) when Byzantine religious and imperial authorities opposed the veneration of icons, causing civil wars and destruction of religious images.

hosios-loukas.name: Hosios Loukas
hosios-loukas.summary: A walled monastery near Distomo in Boeotia, Greece, founded in the mid-10th century and ranked among the most important monuments of Middle Byzantine architecture and art.

daphni-monastery.name: Daphni Monastery
daphni-monastery.summary: An 11th-century Byzantine monastery near Athens, recognized with Hosios Loukas and Nea Moni as a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its gold-ground mosaics and architecture.

cross-in-square.name: Cross-in-square plan
cross-in-square.summary: A church floor plan with a square centre containing an internal cross shape topped by a dome, the dominant style of church architecture in the middle and late Byzantine Empire.

medieval-city-of-rhodes.name: Medieval City of Rhodes
medieval-city-of-rhodes.summary: A UNESCO World Heritage site built between about 1309 and 1523 on the island of Rhodes, with its high town constructed by the Hospitallers within a 4-kilometre wall.

basil-i.name: Basil I
basil-i.summary: Byzantine emperor from 867 to 886, a peasant's son who rose through the imperial court, had his predecessor Michael III assassinated, and founded the Macedonian dynasty.

nea-ekklesia.name: Nea Ekklesia
nea-ekklesia.summary: A church built in Constantinople by Byzantine Emperor Basil I between 876 and 880, the first grand new church there since Hagia Sophia; destroyed in 1490 after a lightning strike.

nea-moni-of-chios.name: Nea Moni of Chios
nea-moni-of-chios.summary: An 11th-century Greek Orthodox monastery on the island of Chios, renowned for mosaics among the finest examples of Macedonian Renaissance art, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1990.

constantine-ix-monomachos.name: Constantine IX
constantine-ix-monomachos.summary: Byzantine emperor from 1042 to 1055 who gained the throne through marriage to Empress Zoë, sharing rule with her sister Theodora during one of the era's most consequential reigns.

macedonian-dynasty.name: Macedonian dynasty
macedonian-dynasty.summary: Byzantine imperial dynasty that ruled from 867 to 1056, a period when the empire reached its greatest extent since the early Muslim conquests and the arts flourished.

pammakaristos-church.name: Pammakaristos Church
pammakaristos-church.summary: A Byzantine church in Istanbul, converted into the Fethiye Mosque in 1591, notable for housing the largest collection of Byzantine mosaics in the city after Hagia Sophia.

parecclesion.name: Parecclesion
parecclesion.summary: A side chapel in early Byzantine churches, used for funerary rites before and after burial and typically decorated with frescoes.

michael-doukas-glabas-tarchaneiotes.name: Michael Glabas Tarchaniotes
michael-doukas-glabas-tarchaneiotes.summary: A Byzantine aristocrat and general (c. 1235–after 1304) who served two emperors in Balkan campaigns and was patron of Constantinople's Pammakaristos Church, where he was buried.

didymoteicho.name: Didymoteicho (Demotika)
didymoteicho.summary: Historical name for the town of Didymoteicho in northeastern Greece, near the borders with Turkey and Bulgaria, with about 8,681 residents in 2021.

orestias.name: Orestias / Adrianople
orestias.summary: An ancient Greek settlement in Thrace, later refounded by Hadrian as Adrianople, near present-day Edirne, Turkey.

skanderbeg.name: Skanderbeg
skanderbeg.summary: An Albanian nobleman, about 1405 to 1468, who led resistance against the Ottomans as ruler of Krujë and later became Albania's national hero.

battle-of-torvioll.name: Battle of Torvioll
battle-of-torvioll.summary: A battle fought on 29 June 1444 in what is now Albania, where Skanderbeg's forces ambushed and defeated an Ottoman army sent by Murad II, boosting Albanian morale against Ottoman rule.

siege-of-kruj-1450.name: Siege of Krujë (1450)
siege-of-kruj-1450.summary: A failed 1450 Ottoman siege of the Albanian town of Krujë led by Sultan Murad II, repelled by Skanderbeg's forces after disease and low morale broke the Ottoman camp.

battle-of-albulena.name: Battle of Albulena
battle-of-albulena.summary: A battle fought on 2 September 1457 in which Albanian forces under Skanderbeg defeated an Ottoman army, despite earlier betrayals by his own officers and his nephew, by dispersing and later reassembling his troops.

lek-dukagjini.name: Lekë Dukagjini
lek-dukagjini.summary: A 15th-century Albanian nobleman who ruled the Principality of Dukagjini from 1446 until the Ottoman conquest in 1479, and a contemporary of Skanderbeg who led resistance after his death. Best known for the customary law code bearing his name.

catalan-company.name: Catalan Company
catalan-company.summary: A band of mercenaries led by Roger de Flor in the early 14th century, hired by the Byzantine emperor and formed from veterans of the Sicilian Vespers war.

duchy-of-athens.name: Duchy of Athens
duchy-of-athens.summary: A Crusader state in Greece covering Attica and Boeotia, founded after the Fourth Crusade in 1205 and ruled successively by French, Catalan and Italian dynasties until Ottoman conquest in 1458.

battle-of-halmyros.name: Battle of Halmyros
battle-of-halmyros.summary: A battle on 15 March 1311 in which the mercenary Catalan Company decisively defeated the Frankish Duchy of Athens under Walter of Brienne, who had hired but refused to pay them.

walter-v-of-brienne.name: Walter of Brienne
walter-v-of-brienne.summary: Duke of Athens from 1308 until 1311, a French nobleman who hired the Catalan Company as mercenaries but refused to pay them, provoking the rebellion that destroyed his army at the Battle of Halmyros.

lala-shahin-pasha.name: Lala Şahin Pasha
lala-shahin-pasha.summary: An Ottoman military commander (c. 1330-1388) and the first Beylerbey of Rumelia, who mentored Sultan Murad I and led key campaigns expanding Ottoman rule into the Balkans.

hac-i-lbey.name: Hacı İlbey
hac-i-lbey.summary: Ottoman commander during the empire's early years, active from around 1305 to 1365 or 1371.

vuka-in-of-serbia.name: Vukašin Mrnjavčević
vuka-in-of-serbia.summary: King of Serbia as co-ruler with Stefan Uroš V from 1365 to 1371, killed alongside his brother at the Battle of Maritsa against the Ottomans in 1371.

jovan-uglje-a.name: Jovan Uglješa
jovan-uglje-a.summary: Serbian medieval nobleman (fl. 1346–1371) who held the title of despot and ruled the Principality of Serres; he was killed at the Battle of Maritsa in 1371 while opposing the advancing Ottomans alongside his brothers Vukašin and Gojko Mrnjavčević.

maritsa.name: Maritsa
maritsa.summary: 480 km river through Thrace in Southeast Europe, the longest running solely within the Balkan peninsula's interior, flowing through Bulgaria and forming part of the Greece–Turkey border.

ottoman-venetian-wars.name: Ottoman–Venetian Wars
ottoman-venetian-wars.summary: Series of conflicts between the Ottoman Empire and the Republic of Venice from 1396 to 1718, through which the Ottomans gradually took Venetian territory, including Thessalonica, Cyprus and Crete.

karl-thopia.name: Karl Thopia
karl-thopia.summary: Albanian feudal prince and warlord (c. 1339-1388) who ruled Albanian domains from 1358 until the first Ottoman conquest of Albania.

nikephoros-ii-orsini.name: Nikephoros II Orsini
nikephoros-ii-orsini.summary: Ruler of the Despotate of Epirus from 1335 to 1338 and again from 1356 until his death in 1359.

despotate-of-epirus.name: Despotate of Epirus
despotate-of-epirus.summary: A Greek successor state of the Byzantine Empire founded in 1204 after the Fourth Crusade, centered on Epirus; it briefly expanded widely before contracting after its 1230 defeat at Klokotnitsa.

achelous-river.name: Achelous River
achelous-river.summary: A 220 km river in western Greece, forming the ancient boundary between Acarnania and Aetolia and revered in antiquity as a river god.

ioannina.name: Ioannina
ioannina.summary: Capital of Epirus in northwestern Greece, traditionally founded by Emperor Justinian in the 6th century; later the seat of Ottoman rule and power base of Ali Pasha until 1867.

prince-marko.name: Prince Marko
prince-marko.summary: De jure Serbian king from 1371 to 1395 and de facto ruler around Prilep in Macedonia, later becoming a major legendary hero in South Slavic oral tradition.

serbian-empire.name: Serbian Empire
serbian-empire.summary: A medieval Serbian state established in 1346 by Dušan the Mighty, the most powerful state in Southeast Europe at the time, stretching from the Danube to the Gulf of Corinth until its end in 1371.

battle-of-maritsa.name: Battle of Maritsa
battle-of-maritsa.summary: A 26 September 1371 battle near the Maritsa River in which Ottoman forces crushed a Serbian coalition, killing both commanders and opening the way for Ottoman expansion into the Balkans.

battle-of-the-golden-spurs.name: Battle of the Golden Spurs
battle-of-the-golden-spurs.summary: A battle on 11 July 1302 near Kortrijk where Flemish civic militia infantry unexpectedly routed French royal cavalry, named for the hundreds of gilded spurs captured from fallen French knights.

preljub.name: Preljub
preljub.summary: Serbian magnate and general who served Emperor Stefan Dušan, taking part in southern conquests and holding Thessaly with the rank of caesar from 1348 to 1356.

aydinids.name: Aydinids
aydinids.summary: A Turkoman principality in western Anatolia known for its seaborne raiding, one of several beyliks that arose in the region.

smyrna.name: Smyrna
smyrna.summary: An ancient Greek city on the Aegean coast of Anatolia, renamed İzmir in 1930, with remains from the Archaic and Roman periods still found within the modern city.

stefan-du-an.name: Stefan Dušan
stefan-du-an.summary: King of Serbia from 1331 and Emperor of the Serbs, Greeks, Bulgarians and Albanians from 1346, under whom Serbia became the most powerful state in Southeast Europe.

macedonia-region.name: Byzantine Macedonia
macedonia-region.summary: In the medieval period, a Byzantine administrative theme named Macedonia was carved out mostly in Thrace, distinct from the wider historical region of the same name.

aleksandar-shopov.name: Aleksandar Shopov
aleksandar-shopov.summary: Historian and assistant professor of early modern Ottoman history at Binghamton University, focused on Ottoman science, technology and environmental history.

boniface-of-verona.name: Boniface of Verona
boniface-of-verona.summary: A Lombard lord in Frankish Greece who expelled the Byzantines from Euboea in 1296, served as regent of the Duchy of Athens, and was captured by the Catalan Company, who offered him leadership.

roger-deslaur.name: Roger Deslaur
roger-deslaur.summary: Knight from Roussillon who survived the Battle of Halmyros in 1311 and became rector and marshal of the Catalan Company after Boniface of Verona declined the post.

frederick-iii-of-sicily.name: Frederick III of Sicily
frederick-iii-of-sicily.summary: King of Sicily from 1295 until his death in 1337, also called Frederick II, who fought in the War of the Sicilian Vespers and was confirmed as king by the 1302 Peace of Caltabellotta.

manfred-of-athens.name: Manfred of Athens
manfred-of-athens.summary: A son of Frederick III of Sicily, named Duke of Athens and Neopatria at age five in 1312 but died in a riding accident before turning twelve, never having visited his realm.

alfonso-fadrique.name: Alfonso Fadrique
alfonso-fadrique.summary: Illegitimate son of Frederick II of Sicily who served as vicar general of the Duchy of Athens from 1317 to 1330 and conquered Neopatras and Thessaly, becoming Vicar General of the Duchy of Neopatras.

digenes-akritas.name: Digenes Akritas
digenes-akritas.summary: Medieval Greek epic poem from 12th-century Byzantium about a frontier warrior of mixed Greek and Arab descent, regarded as the only surviving Byzantine epic and an early landmark of vernacular Greek literature.

attic-greek.name: Attic Greek
attic-greek.summary: The ancient Greek dialect of Athens and Attica, often called Classical Greek, the prestige form taught to students and the basis of later Koine Greek.

koine-greek.name: Koine Greek
koine-greek.summary: The common form of Greek spoken and written across the Hellenistic world, Roman Empire and early Byzantine Empire, spreading after Alexander the Great's conquests and used for the Septuagint and New Testament.

acritic-songs.name: Acritic songs
acritic-songs.summary: Byzantine epic poems from around the ninth century celebrating frontier guards who fought in the Arab–Byzantine wars; includes the famous Digenes Akritas.

the-chronicle-of-morea.name: The Chronicle of the Morea
the-chronicle-of-morea.summary: A 14th-century verse chronicle, surviving in French, Greek, Italian and Aragonese versions, narrating the Franks' establishment of feudalism in the Peloponnese after the Fourth Crusade.

frankokratia.name: Frankokratia
frankokratia.summary: Period of Western European, chiefly French and Venetian, rule over former Byzantine lands after the 1204 Fourth Crusade, lasting in places until the Ottoman conquest.

principality-of-achaea.name: Principality of Achaea
principality-of-achaea.summary: A vassal state of the Latin Empire covering the Peloponnese after the Fourth Crusade; it became the dominant Frankish power in Greece for over two centuries.

alexiad.name: Alexiad
alexiad.summary: A medieval historical and biographical text written around 1148 by the Byzantine princess Anna Komnene about her father's reign, in artificial Attic Greek. It documents Byzantine history and its clashing views with the West during the Crusades.

alexios-i-komnenos.name: Alexios I Komnenos
alexios-i-komnenos.summary: Byzantine emperor from 1081 to 1118 who seized the throne by rebellion and reversed the empire's decline. His appeal to Western Europe for help against the Seljuk Turks helped spark the First Crusade.

michael-psellos.name: Michael Psellos
michael-psellos.summary: Byzantine monk, scholar, philosopher and historian (c. 1018–c. 1096) who advised several emperors and wrote the Chronographia, a key source on 11th-century Byzantine history.

komnenos.name: Komnenos dynasty
komnenos.summary: A Byzantine Greek noble family that ruled the Byzantine Empire from 1081 to 1185 and later founded the Empire of Trebizond, which they ruled until 1461.

political-verse.name: Versus politicus
political-verse.summary: A 15-syllable iambic verse form used in Greek poetry since Byzantine times; despite its name, it has no political content, deriving instead from a Greek word meaning civic or secular.

john-vi-kantakouzenos.name: John VI Kantakouzenos
john-vi-kantakouzenos.summary: Byzantine emperor (1292–1383) who reigned 1347–1354 after serving as regent; his civil wars cost Byzantium territory and let the Ottomans first gain a foothold in Europe.

nicephorus-gregoras.name: Nicephorus Gregoras
nicephorus-gregoras.summary: Byzantine astronomer, historian and theologian (c. 1295 – c. 1360) whose 37-volume Roman History is a primary source for 14th-century events.

trebuchet.name: Counterweight trebuchet
trebuchet.summary: A siege engine using a counterweight to swing its arm, more powerful than the earlier manpower-driven trebuchet, that appeared around the Mediterranean in the 12th century and was later carried to China by the Mongols.

galen.name: Galen
galen.summary: A Roman-era Greek physician, surgeon, and philosopher (129–c.216 CE) whose anatomical writings, shaped by the four-humors theory, dominated Western medicine for over 1,300 years.

gregory-chioniades.name: Gregory Chioniades
gregory-chioniades.summary: A Byzantine astronomer (about 1240 to about 1320) who traveled to Persia to study its astronomy and mathematics, then founded an astronomical academy at Trebizond and served as Orthodox bishop of Tabriz.

trabzon.name: Trabzon
trabzon.summary: City on Turkey's Black Sea coast, founded in 756 BC by Greek colonists, later capital of the Byzantine successor Empire of Trebizond before falling to the Ottomans in 1461.

maragheh-observatory.name: Maragheh observatory
maragheh-observatory.summary: A 13th-century astronomical observatory in Persia, founded under the Ilkhanid ruler Hulagu and directed by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, considered one of the most advanced scientific institutions in Eurasia.

nasir-al-din-al-tusi.name: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi
nasir-al-din-al-tusi.summary: A Persian polymath (1201–1274) who advanced astronomy and trigonometry, created influential planetary tables, and is regarded as one of medieval Islam's greatest scientists.

zij-i-ilkhani.name: Zij-i Ilkhani
zij-i-ilkhani.summary: A set of astronomical tables compiled by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi and his team at the Maragha observatory, completed in 1272 after twelve years of observations.

handy-tables.name: Handy Tables
handy-tables.summary: A set of astronomical tables the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy compiled after the Almagest, simplified for practical use and influential through late antiquity and medieval times.

almagest.name: Almagest
almagest.summary: Ptolemy's 2nd-century astronomical treatise that established the geocentric model of the universe, accepted for over 1,200 years.

theodore-metochites.name: Theodore Metochites
theodore-metochites.summary: Byzantine statesman, author and philosopher-astronomer (1270–1332) who served as chief adviser to Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos from about 1305 to 1328.

manuel-bryennios.name: Manuel Bryennios
manuel-bryennios.summary: A Byzantine scholar active in Constantinople around 1300, teaching astronomy, mathematics and music theory; his surviving work Harmonika codifies Byzantine musical scholarship drawing on classical Greek authors.

tusi-couple.name: Tusi couple
tusi-couple.summary: A mathematical device of two nested circles that makes a point move back and forth in a straight line, devised by 13th-century Persian astronomer Nasir al-Din al-Tusi to explain planetary motion.

andronikos-ii-palaiologos.name: Andronikos II Palaiologos
andronikos-ii-palaiologos.summary: Byzantine emperor from 1282 to 1328, whose reign began the empire's final decline as the Turks conquered its remaining Anatolian territories and he was later forced to abdicate after civil war with his own grandson.

pope-gregory-xiii.name: Pope Gregory XIII
pope-gregory-xiii.summary: Born Ugo Boncompagni, head of the Catholic Church from 1572 to 1585; best known for commissioning the Gregorian calendar still used today.

nicomachus.name: Nicomachus
nicomachus.summary: Greek Neopythagorean philosopher (c. 60–120 AD) whose writings on arithmetic and music became standard textbooks into the medieval period.

nicholas-myrepsos.name: Nicholas Myrepsos
nicholas-myrepsos.summary: Byzantine physician active around 1240–1280, known chiefly for a medical compendium that still survives.

john-iii-doukas-vatatzes.name: John III Doukas Vatatzes
john-iii-doukas-vatatzes.summary: Emperor of Nicaea from 1221 to 1254, succeeded by his son Theodore II Doukas Laskaris.

actuarius.name: actuarius
actuarius.summary: Byzantine and late Roman official title, originally for distributing military pay, later applied to prominent court physicians from around the 11th–12th century.

serbian-orthodox-church.name: Serbian Orthodox Church
serbian-orthodox-church.summary: An Eastern Orthodox church covering the Balkans, first made an autocephalous archbishopric in 1219 under Saint Sava and elevated to a patriarchate in 1346, led by the Serbian patriarch.

isaac-ii-angelos.name: Isaac II Angelos
isaac-ii-angelos.summary: Byzantine Emperor from 1185 to 1195 and co-emperor with his son from 1203 to 1204, who seized the throne in an 1185 revolt and founded the Angelos imperial dynasty.

alexios-v-doukas.name: Alexios V Doukas
alexios-v-doukas.summary: Byzantine emperor for a few months in early 1204, who took power by coup just before the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople. He was later blinded by his father-in-law and executed by the new Latin rulers.

stefan-de-anski.name: Stefan Dečanski
stefan-de-anski.summary: King of Serbia from 1322 to 1331, son of King Milutin, who defeated rival claimants to the throne and built the Visoki Dečani monastery.

stefan-uro-v.name: Stefan Uroš V
stefan-uro-v.summary: The second Emperor (Tsar) of the Serbian Empire from 1355 to 1371, and before that Serbian King and co-ruler with his father Stefan Dušan from 1346; known as Uroš the Weak.

asen-dynasty.name: Asen dynasty
asen-dynasty.summary: A medieval Bulgarian ruling family that founded the Second Bulgarian Empire after an anti-Byzantine rebellion in 1185, ruling it until 1280.

second-bulgarian-empire.name: Second Bulgarian Empire
second-bulgarian-empire.summary: A medieval Bulgarian state lasting from 1185 to 1396, dominant in the Balkans under Tsars Kaloyan and Ivan Asen II before its gradual conquest by the Ottomans.

lazar-of-serbia.name: Lazar Hrebeljanović
lazar-of-serbia.summary: Medieval Serbian ruler, about 1329 to 1389, who built the powerful state of Moravian Serbia and died leading Christian forces at the Battle of Kosovo.

stefan-lazarevi.name: Stefan Lazarević
stefan-lazarevi.summary: Serbian prince from 1389 and later despot from 1402 until 1427, regarded as one of the finest knights of his time, who ruled first as an Ottoman vassal and then as a Hungarian ally.

despotate-of-the-morea.name: Despotate of the Morea
despotate-of-the-morea.summary: A Byzantine province covering the Peloponnese, usually ruled by relatives of the reigning emperor; its capital, Mystras, became a center of the Palaiologan Renaissance.

navarrese-company.name: Navarrese Company
navarrese-company.summary: A band of mercenaries, mostly from Navarre and Gascony, that fought in Albania and Greece in the late 14th and early 15th centuries as Frankish power in the region waned.

kingdom-of-naples.name: Kingdom of Naples
kingdom-of-naples.summary: A state ruling southern Italy from 1282 to 1816, formed after the War of the Sicilian Vespers and later contested by France and Spain before coming under Spanish control by 1504.

pope-innocent-iii.name: Pope Innocent III
pope-innocent-iii.summary: One of the most powerful medieval popes, ruling the Catholic Church and Papal States from 1198 to 1216, who greatly expanded the Crusades and reformed canon law.

kaloyan-of-bulgaria.name: Kaloyan
kaloyan-of-bulgaria.summary: Emperor of Bulgaria from 1196 to 1207, brother of the leaders of Bulgaria's independence uprising; he defeated Byzantine forces at Varna in 1201 and took the title 'the Roman-Slayer.'

constantine-i-tih.name: Constantine Tikh
constantine-i-tih.summary: Tsar of Bulgaria from 1257 to 1277 who fought wars with the Byzantine Empire and Hungary and was later paralyzed from the waist down.

george-i-of-bulgaria.name: George I Terter
george-i-of-bulgaria.summary: George I Terter: Member of the Terter dynasty who ruled as tsar of Bulgaria from 1280 to 1292; he died in 1308 or 1309.

michael-shishman-of-bulgaria.name: Michael Shishman
michael-shishman-of-bulgaria.summary: Tsar of Bulgaria from 1323 to 1330 and founder of the Shishman dynasty, who died leading an aggressive foreign policy at the disastrous Battle of Velbazhd.

pope-leo-ix.name: Pope Leo IX
pope-leo-ix.summary: Bishop of Rome and ruler of the Papal States from 1049 to 1054, whose reforming papacy helped precipitate the 1054 split between the Catholic and Orthodox Churches.

east-west-schism.name: East-West Schism
east-west-schism.summary: The 1054 break in communion between the Catholic Church and the Eastern Orthodox Church, following centuries of theological and political disputes between the Greek East and Latin West.

gemistos-plethon.name: Gemistos Plethon
gemistos-plethon.summary: A Greek scholar and philosopher of the late Byzantine era (c. 1355-1454) who reintroduced Plato's ideas to Western Europe at the Council of Florence and helped spark the Florentine Renaissance.

mystras.name: Mystras
mystras.summary: A fortified Byzantine town in the Peloponnese that served as capital of the Despotate of the Morea in the 14th and 15th centuries and drew artists and scholars; now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

bogomilism.name: Bogomilism
bogomilism.summary: A Christian dualist sect founded in the First Bulgarian Empire in the 10th century that rejected church hierarchy and spread through the Balkans and Byzantine Empire.

saint-sava.name: Saint Sava
saint-sava.summary: Serbian prince born Rastko Nemanjić (1169 or 1174 to 1235) who became a monk, founded the monastery of Hilandar, wrote Serbia's first law code, and is considered one of the greatest figures of Serbian medieval literature.

stefan-the-first-crowned.name: Stefan the First-Crowned
stefan-the-first-crowned.summary: Grand Prince of Serbia from 1196 and its first king, from 1217 until his death in 1228, who transformed the Grand Principality into a kingdom and helped his brother Saint Sava found the Serbian Orthodox Church.

nemanji-dynasty.name: Nemanjić dynasty
nemanji-dynasty.summary: Serbia's most prominent medieval royal house, producing twelve monarchs from 1166 to 1371 and overseeing the kingdom's rise to an empire under Stefan Dušan.

tsakonia.name: Tsakonia
tsakonia.summary: Small region in the eastern Peloponnese where the Tsakonian language is spoken; not a formal political entity of modern Greece.

maniots.name: Maniots
maniots.summary: The traditional native Greek inhabitants of the Mani Peninsula in the southern Peloponnese, historically known as fierce, independent warriors who claim descent from the ancient Spartans.

bosnian-church.name: Bosnian Church
bosnian-church.summary: A Christian church in medieval Bosnia (13th–15th centuries) deemed heretical by the Pope, known mainly through Catholic anti-heretical writings since few of its own records survive.

banate-of-bosnia.name: Banate of Bosnia
banate-of-bosnia.summary: A medieval state in what is now Bosnia and Herzegovina, founded in the mid-12th century and effectively independent despite Hungarian claims, marked by conflict over the heretical Bosnian Church, until becoming a kingdom in 1377.

pope-innocent-iv.name: Pope Innocent IV
pope-innocent-iv.summary: Head of the Catholic Church and Papal States from 1243 to 1254, a noted canonist whose dispute with Emperor Frederick II forced him to flee to France; he later authorized torture against heretics.

ste-ak.name: Stećci
ste-ak.summary: Monumental medieval tombstones found across Bosnia and Herzegovina and nearby parts of Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia, in use from the mid 12th century. UNESCO added them to the World Heritage List in 2016.

meteora.name: Meteora
meteora.summary: Rock formation in Thessaly, northwestern Greece, hosting one of the most prominent complexes of Eastern Orthodox monasteries. It joined the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1988.

simeon-uro.name: Simeon Uroš
simeon-uro.summary: Self-proclaimed Emperor of Serbs and Greeks from 1356 to 1370, ruling a separate state centred on Thessaly and Epirus. Half-brother of Stephen Dušan, he seized the chance to claim power after Dušan died in 1355.

hesychasm.name: Hesychasm
hesychasm.summary: Contemplative monastic tradition in Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches, rooted in early Christian monasticism.

jesus-prayer.name: Jesus Prayer
jesus-prayer.summary: Short prayer, "Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner," most common in Eastern Christianity. It is repeated continually as part of ascetic practice, especially within hesychasm.

uncreated-light.name: Uncreated Light
uncreated-light.summary: Eastern Orthodox teaching that the light seen on Mount Tabor at Jesus's Transfiguration was divine and not created. Gregory Palamas formulated it in the 14th century, and it became official Orthodox doctrine in 1347.

gregory-palamas.name: Gregory Palamas
gregory-palamas.summary: Byzantine Greek theologian (c. 1296-1359), monk of Mount Athos and later archbishop of Thessalonica. He defended hesychast spirituality and has been venerated as a saint in the Eastern Orthodox Church since 1368.

athanasius-the-meteorite.name: Athanasios the Meteorite
athanasius-the-meteorite.summary: Christian monk who lived from 1302 to 1380 and is a saint of the Eastern Orthodox Church. He is best known as founder of the Great Meteoron monastery in Meteora, Greece.

monastery-of-great-meteoron.name: Great Meteoron
monastery-of-great-meteoron.summary: Greek Orthodox monastery near Kalambaka in central Greece, perched on a rocky precipice over 415 metres above the Pineios valley. It is one of the oldest of the Meteora monasteries, listed by UNESCO in 1988.

tvrtko-i-of-bosnia.name: Tvrtko I
tvrtko-i-of-bosnia.summary: First king of Bosnia (c. 1338–1391), who became ban in 1353, crowned himself king in 1377 claiming Serbia's throne too, and brought Bosnia's power to its height.

republic-of-ragusa.name: Republic of Ragusa
republic-of-ragusa.summary: An aristocratic maritime republic centered on Dubrovnik, known as Ragusa in Italian and Latin, that existed from 1358 until conquered by Napoleon's forces in 1806-08.

apostolos-vacalopoulos.name: Apostolos Vacalopoulos
apostolos-vacalopoulos.summary: Greek historian (1909-2000) specializing in the Byzantine Empire, Ottoman Greece and modern Greek history, regarded as one of the 20th century's greatest Greek historians.

kallistos-ware.name: Kallistos Ware
kallistos-ware.summary: English bishop and theologian (1934–2022) of the Eastern Orthodox Church, among its best-known modern thinkers. He taught Eastern Orthodox studies at the University of Oxford from 1966 to 2001.

gregory-of-sinai.name: Gregory of Sinai
gregory-of-sinai.summary: Greek Christian monk and writer from Smyrna (c. 1260s-1346), instrumental in the emergence of hesychasm on Mount Athos in the early 14th century.

philotheou-monastery.name: Philotheou Monastery
philotheou-monastery.summary: Eastern Orthodox monastery on the north-eastern side of the Mount Athos peninsula, in the monastic state of Mount Athos in Greece.

bellevaux-abbey.name: Bellevaux Abbey
bellevaux-abbey.summary: Cistercian monastery founded in 1120 in Franche-Comté, France, and suppressed in 1790. Its lords' allies gave it the sacked Daphni Monastery in Greece shortly after 1205.

greece_balkans-medieval-art-004: Palace of the Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes
